subtopic_detail: Metabolic monitoring schedule after commencing an atypical antipsychotic
stem:
You are the community mental health registrar reviewing a 24 year old man 12 weeks after starting olanzapine 15 mg nocte for a first episode of psychosis. Symptoms have settled and he is back at his TAFE course.

He reports his appetite is bigger and his trousers feel tighter around the waist. He has no cardiac symptoms and no personal or family history of diabetes or heart disease. He does not smoke and drinks alcohol only on weekends.

On assessment his weight has risen from 74 kg at baseline to 82 kg and his waist circumference from 88 cm to 96 cm. Blood pressure is 128/78, pulse 76 regular. He is not fasting today; a random glucose taken at baseline was 4.9 mmol/L and baseline fasting lipids and HbA1c were within normal limits.

data_table.Anthropometry: Weight 82 kg (baseline 74 kg); waist 96 cm (baseline 88 cm); BMI 26.9
data_table.Baseline metabolic screen (0 weeks): Fasting glucose 4.9 mmol/L; HbA1c 5.4%; total cholesterol 4.2 mmol/L; LDL 2.6 mmol/L; triglycerides 1.1 mmol/L
data_table.Medications: Olanzapine 15 mg nocte for 12 weeks; no other regular medications

lead_in: What is the most appropriate metabolic monitoring plan now?

options.text: Send serum prolactin as a primary metabolic marker instead of glucose and lipids in this age group
options.rationale: Prolactin is checked when there are hyperprolactinaemia symptoms or on high-prolactinaemia agents (risperidone, amisulpride); it does not replace glucose and lipid surveillance which is the priority on olanzapine (Source: eTG Psychotropic; AMH).

options.text: Defer repeat metabolic bloods until the 12 month mark and rely on weight and waist trend in the interim
options.rationale: 12 week bloods are a specified checkpoint on all antipsychotics; deferring to 12 months misses early-onset dysglycaemia and dyslipidaemia which are highest risk on olanzapine (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG).

options.text: Order fasting glucose and lipids now but omit HbA1c as it is not validated for antipsychotic induced dysglycaemia
options.rationale: HbA1c is explicitly recommended in the RANZCP monitoring schedule alongside fasting glucose; either can be used to screen and both are covered by MBS for this indication (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG).

options.text: Add a random troponin and a resting ECG to the panel as part of routine 12 week antipsychotic screening
options.rationale: Baseline and follow-up ECG is only routine for certain agents (e.g. ziprasidone, high-dose haloperidol, clozapine); troponin has no role in routine metabolic monitoring for olanzapine (Source: eTG Psychotropic).

options.text: Repeat fasting glucose, HbA1c and a fasting lipid profile at this 12 week visit and continue anthropometry each review
options.rationale: RANZCP and eTG Psychotropic recommend fasting glucose or HbA1c and a fasting lipid profile at baseline, 12 weeks, then at least yearly on any antipsychotic; weight and waist are checked at every review with early rise on olanzapine a specific trigger for lifestyle intervention and consideration of agent switch (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Schizophrenia; eTG Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: On any antipsychotic the RANZCP monitoring schedule sets metabolic bloods at baseline, 12 weeks, then at least yearly, plus weight and waist at every review. Early weight gain on olanzapine is a specific trigger to repeat glucose/HbA1c and fasting lipids and to consider a switch.
key_points: Baseline, 12 week and at least annual fasting glucose/HbA1c and lipids on all antipsychotics.
Weight and waist every review; >=7% weight gain triggers intervention.
Prolactin and ECG are agent-specific, not universal.
explanation.pearls: Olanzapine and clozapine carry the highest metabolic burden; the 12 week bloods catch early dysglycaemia before overt diabetes.

subtopic_detail: Interpreting weight gain and switching agent on olanzapine
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a community clinic. A 27 year old woman has been on olanzapine 20 mg nocte for 9 months for a schizoaffective disorder. She is symptomatically well and back at work as a barista.

Baseline before starting olanzapine: weight 62 kg, BMI 22.8, waist 76 cm, fasting glucose 4.6 mmol/L, HbA1c 5.3%, LDL 2.4 mmol/L, triglycerides 1.0 mmol/L. She has no personal history of diabetes but her mother developed type 2 diabetes at 55. She does not smoke.

At today's visit she weighs 71 kg (BMI 26.1), waist 87 cm, blood pressure 122/78. Fasting bloods this morning: glucose 5.4 mmol/L, HbA1c 5.6%, LDL 3.1 mmol/L, triglycerides 1.4 mmol/L. She has tried a dietitian and a gym program for 3 months without further weight loss. She is anxious about further weight gain and would like a plan.

data_table.Anthropometry: Weight 71 kg (baseline 62 kg, +14.5%); waist 87 cm (baseline 76 cm); BMI 26.1
data_table.Fasting bloods now: Glucose 5.4 mmol/L; HbA1c 5.6%; LDL 3.1 mmol/L; triglycerides 1.4 mmol/L
data_table.Medications: Olanzapine 20 mg nocte for 9 months; no other medications

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her pharmacological management?

options.text: Continue olanzapine at the current dose and defer repeat metabolic bloods until the routine annual review in 12 months
options.rationale: A weight gain of >7% with progressive metabolic drift plus a first-degree family history of type 2 diabetes triggers active management rather than watchful waiting (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG).

options.text: Cross-titrate olanzapine to aripiprazole while continuing lifestyle measures and repeating metabolic bloods after the switch is complete
options.rationale: Aripiprazole has the most favourable metabolic profile among second-generation antipsychotics; switching after failed lifestyle intervention in a patient with >7% weight gain and worsening lipids is the recommended step, with a cross-titration to preserve symptom control (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG; eTG Psychotropic).

options.text: Add metformin 500 mg twice daily to olanzapine and defer any change of antipsychotic agent for now
options.rationale: Adjunctive metformin has modest evidence for attenuating antipsychotic-induced weight gain but is considered when a switch is not feasible; here the primary lever is agent switch given her preferences and progressive drift (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG).

options.text: Reduce olanzapine to 10 mg nocte and monitor for symptom relapse whilst continuing lifestyle measures
options.rationale: Dose reduction of olanzapine has an inconsistent effect on weight and risks relapse of a stabilised psychosis; switching to a metabolically neutral agent addresses the mechanism more reliably (Source: eTG Psychotropic).

options.text: Cross-titrate olanzapine to clozapine because the metabolic burden is comparable and it improves adherence
options.rationale: Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant illness and carries an equal or greater metabolic burden than olanzapine; it is not indicated as a metabolic-friendly switch (Source: eTG Psychotropic; AMH).

explanation.summary: Persistent >7% weight gain and worsening lipids and glucose on olanzapine, despite lifestyle intervention, is a trigger to switch to a metabolically neutral antipsychotic such as aripiprazole. Cross-titration protects the stabilised illness while lifestyle measures continue.
key_points: Metabolic switch threshold: >7% weight gain, worsening lipids or dysglycaemia after adequate lifestyle trial.
Aripiprazole has the most favourable metabolic profile among SGAs.
Clozapine is not a metabolic-neutral alternative.
explanation.pearls: Adjunctive metformin is second-line to a switch when the current agent cannot be changed (e.g. clozapine responder).

subtopic_detail: Hyperprolactinaemia workup on risperidone
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a community clinic. A 32 year old woman on risperidone 4 mg daily for 8 months for schizophrenia presents with 6 weeks of non-cyclical breast tenderness, milky bilateral nipple discharge, and secondary amenorrhoea. She has previously had regular cycles and is not sexually active.

She has no headaches, visual changes, weight loss or heat intolerance and is not on other regular medications. Home pregnancy test yesterday was negative. She is symptomatically well from a psychiatric standpoint and has partial insight into her illness.

On examination she is not distressed. Blood pressure is 118/72, pulse 72 regular. Visual fields to confrontation are full. Serum prolactin is 2400 mIU/L (reference <500), TSH 1.8 mIU/L, morning cortisol within normal limits, and beta hCG negative.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral galactorrhoea; visual fields full; no goitre or thyromegaly
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 2400 mIU/L (<500); TSH 1.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0); morning cortisol within normal limits; beta hCG negative
data_table.Medications: Risperidone 4 mg daily for 8 months; no other medications

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Order an urgent MRI pituitary before any change in psychotropic therapy because of the risk of adenoma
options.rationale: MRI is reserved for prolactin above ~2500 mIU/L after drug cessation or when clinical features suggest a pituitary lesion; imaging first is not the appropriate initial step when a plausible drug cause is present (Source: eTG Endocrinology).

options.text: Reduce risperidone to 2 mg daily and repeat prolactin in 6 weeks if symptoms are unchanged with dose reduction
options.rationale: Risperidone-induced prolactin elevation is often persistent even at lower doses and dose reduction risks symptom relapse; switching to a prolactin-sparing agent is more reliable (Source: eTG Psychotropic).

options.text: Add cabergoline 0.25 mg twice weekly while continuing risperidone at the current dose to normalise prolactin
options.rationale: Dopamine agonists risk destabilising the psychosis by pharmacological antagonism of the antipsychotic; they are not first line in drug-induced hyperprolactinaemia in patients with schizophrenia (Source: eTG Psychotropic).

options.text: Cross-titrate risperidone to aripiprazole and reassess prolactin and symptoms 6 weeks after the switch is complete
options.rationale: Symptomatic drug-induced hyperprolactinaemia is best managed by switching to a prolactin-sparing agent such as aripiprazole; prolactin normalises within weeks and reassessment then determines whether MRI is needed (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG; eTG Psychotropic).

options.text: Continue risperidone unchanged and refer to endocrinology for consideration of oestrogen replacement therapy
options.rationale: Oestrogen replacement is only considered after the drug cause has been addressed and hypogonadism persists; it is not the first response to symptomatic drug-induced hyperprolactinaemia (Source: eTG Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: Symptomatic hyperprolactinaemia on risperidone (galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea) is best managed by switching to a prolactin-sparing antipsychotic such as aripiprazole, then reassessing prolactin. MRI is reserved for persistent elevation off the offending drug or for red-flag features.
key_points: Risperidone, paliperidone, and amisulpride are the highest prolactin agents.
Aripiprazole is prolactin-sparing and can also be added at low dose to lower prolactin without switching if needed.
MRI pituitary if prolactin remains elevated after switch or if red-flag features.
explanation.pearls: Dopamine agonists in patients on antipsychotics can trigger relapse; avoid unless endocrine consultation.

subtopic_detail: Long-term surveillance schedule for lithium
stem:
You are the GP registrar seeing a 42 year old woman who is 18 months into lithium prophylaxis for bipolar I disorder. She has been well with no admissions since starting lithium and takes her dose reliably.

Her most recent trough lithium level (12 hours post dose) is 0.7 mmol/L, taken 6 months ago. She has no polyuria, polydipsia, tremor, ataxia, or heat intolerance. She takes no other regular medications, is not planning pregnancy, and drinks 1.5 litres of fluid daily.

On assessment blood pressure is 122/76, pulse 74 regular. Weight is stable at 68 kg. She asks how often she now needs bloods and what tests should be done.

data_table.Most recent bloods (6 months ago): Lithium 0.7 mmol/L (0.6-0.8 target); eGFR 92 mL/min/1.73m2; TSH 2.1 mIU/L; corrected calcium 2.35 mmol/L
data_table.Medications: Lithium 750 mg nocte; no other regular medications

lead_in: What is the most appropriate long-term monitoring plan?

options.text: Trough lithium level yearly with renal function only when clinical concern arises about toxicity or dehydration
options.rationale: Yearly-only lithium levels miss subclinical drift; renal function must be tracked routinely because chronic lithium nephropathy is often silent and irreversible if missed (Source: eTG Psychotropic).

options.text: Trough lithium level every 3 to 6 months and eGFR, TSH and corrected calcium every 6 to 12 months
options.rationale: eTG Psychotropic and RANZCP mood disorders CPG recommend trough lithium every 3-6 months once stable, plus renal function, thyroid function and calcium at 6-12 monthly intervals for the duration of therapy (Source: eTG Psychotropic; RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG).

options.text: Trough lithium level every 3 months plus quarterly parathyroid hormone in place of corrected calcium
options.rationale: Corrected calcium is the standard first-line surveillance for lithium-induced hyperparathyroidism; PTH is checked only if calcium is elevated (Source: eTG Psychotropic).

options.text: Trough lithium level every 6 weeks and 24 hour urinary volume routinely to screen for nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
options.rationale: 6-weekly levels are used during dose titration; 24 hour urine is not routine and is triggered by polyuria or polydipsia (Source: eTG Psychotropic).

options.text: Trough lithium and full blood count every 3 months in place of thyroid function surveillance whilst on therapy
options.rationale: Lithium does not require FBC surveillance and does not replace TFTs, which detect hypothyroidism in around a quarter of long-term users (Source: eTG Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Long-term lithium monitoring is trough level every 3-6 months once stable, plus renal function, thyroid function and corrected calcium every 6-12 months. This catches nephropathy, hypothyroidism, and hyperparathyroidism early.
key_points: Trough level = 12 h post dose.
Prophylaxis target 0.6-0.8 mmol/L (0.8-1.0 for acute mania in some).
Corrected calcium is first-line; PTH is second-line if calcium elevated.
explanation.pearls: Any acute illness with vomiting, diarrhoea, dehydration, new NSAID, ACEi/ARB, or diuretic warrants an ad hoc lithium level.

subtopic_detail: Interpreting lithium level in the context of new medication
stem:
You are the ED registrar. A 58 year old man on lithium 1000 mg nocte for 15 years for bipolar I disorder is brought in by his wife after 3 days of unsteady walking, coarse hand tremor and slurred speech. He is normally independent.

Two weeks ago his GP started perindopril 4 mg for newly diagnosed hypertension. He has had no vomiting or diarrhoea but has been drinking less water than usual during a hot spell. He denies any deliberate overdose and his wife confirms the prescription bottle count matches expected use.

On assessment he is oriented to person only. Pulse is 88 regular, blood pressure 138/86, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.8. There is a coarse resting tremor of the hands, gait ataxia and horizontal nystagmus. Serum lithium 2.4 mmol/L (target 0.6-0.8), creatinine 132 micromol/L (baseline 82), eGFR 46 mL/min/1.73m2, sodium 141, potassium 4.2, corrected calcium 2.36. ECG shows sinus rhythm with a QTc of 460 ms.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 regular, BP 138/86, RR 18, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Neuro exam: Oriented to person only; coarse resting tremor; gait ataxia; horizontal nystagmus
data_table.Bloods: Lithium 2.4 mmol/L (0.6-0.8); creatinine 132 micromol/L (baseline 82); eGFR 46; sodium 141; potassium 4.2; corrected calcium 2.36
data_table.Medications: Lithium 1000 mg nocte for 15 years; perindopril 4 mg daily started 2 weeks ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Withhold lithium, commence intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride at maintenance and repeat lithium level in 6 hours
options.rationale: IV saline alone is inadequate for chronic toxicity with neurological features and level >2.5-3 mmol/L range; renal replacement therapy is the definitive treatment when neurological signs are present with impaired clearance (Source: eTG Toxicology; Australia and New Zealand Poisons Information Centres).

options.text: Administer activated charcoal 50 g orally and repeat 4 hourly while withholding lithium and perindopril
options.rationale: Charcoal does not bind lithium; it has no role in lithium toxicity of any severity (Source: eTG Toxicology).

options.text: Withhold lithium and perindopril, commence intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride and arrange urgent haemodialysis with nephrology
options.rationale: Chronic lithium toxicity with neurological features (ataxia, confusion, nystagmus) and impaired renal function meets EXTRIP consensus criteria for haemodialysis regardless of the precise level; ACEi and dehydration precipitated toxicity by reducing lithium clearance (Source: EXTRIP lithium recommendations; eTG Toxicology).

options.text: Give intravenous sodium polystyrene sulfonate and forced alkaline diuresis with sodium bicarbonate infusion
options.rationale: Sodium polystyrene sulfonate is not indicated for lithium; forced alkaline diuresis increases sodium load without improving lithium clearance and risks fluid overload (Source: eTG Toxicology).

options.text: Continue lithium at a reduced dose of 500 mg nocte, stop perindopril and repeat level in 48 hours
options.rationale: Continuing lithium during established toxicity risks worsening neurotoxicity even with dose reduction; the drug must be withheld and clearance actively enhanced (Source: eTG Toxicology).

explanation.summary: Chronic lithium toxicity with neurological features (ataxia, confusion, nystagmus) plus impaired renal function meets EXTRIP criteria for haemodialysis even at levels below the classical 4.0 mmol/L threshold. ACEi and volume depletion are recognised precipitants.
key_points: Haemodialysis: level >4.0 OR level >2.5 with neurological features/renal impairment OR unable to excrete due to renal failure.
Chronic toxicity presents with neurology at lower levels than acute overdose.
Charcoal does not bind lithium.
explanation.pearls: Whenever an ACEi, ARB, thiazide, or NSAID is started in a lithium patient, check a level within 1-2 weeks.

subtopic_detail: Contraception planning for a woman of childbearing potential on valproate
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 22 year old woman with bipolar I disorder who has been well for 2 years on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily. She has never been pregnant, is in a new relationship, and uses condoms inconsistently. She hopes to have children in the next 5 years but not immediately.

Her weight is 62 kg. Blood pressure is 118/74, pulse 72 regular. She has no history of migraine, VTE, hypertension, or smoking. Liver enzymes, full blood count and beta hCG are within normal limits today. She does not wish to change her mood stabiliser as she has previously failed lithium and lamotrigine trials.

data_table.Investigations: LFTs, FBC within normal limits; beta hCG negative
data_table.Medications: Sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for 2 years
data_table.History: No smoking, no migraine, no VTE, no hypertension

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step to comply with the Australian valproate pregnancy prevention program?

options.text: Switch valproate to carbamazepine 400 mg daily as a safer mood stabiliser option during her fertile years
options.rationale: Carbamazepine is also Category D with an appreciable neural tube defect risk and enzyme-induction interactions; substituting one Category D agent for another does not solve the problem (Source: AMH).

options.text: Continue valproate and advise continued condom use with review of contraception if she becomes sexually active
options.rationale: Condoms alone do not meet the highly effective threshold required by the TGA program; the risk of unplanned pregnancy with a Category D teratogen is unacceptable (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program).

options.text: Continue valproate and start high-dose folic acid 5 mg daily as sufficient risk mitigation without changing contraception
options.rationale: Folate does not mitigate the specific teratogenic risk of valproate (neural tube defects, cognitive impairment, autism spectrum) which persists despite supplementation; contraception is the primary intervention (Source: AMH).

options.text: Provide written information about teratogenicity and arrange a highly effective contraception method before continuing valproate
options.rationale: The TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program requires documented annual counselling, use of a highly effective contraceptive method (LARC preferred: IUD or implant), and signed acknowledgement in any woman of childbearing potential remaining on valproate (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program; AMH).

options.text: Stop valproate abruptly and start lithium 500 mg nocte pending contraception planning at the next visit
options.rationale: She has already failed lithium and abrupt discontinuation of a stabilising agent risks manic relapse; the priority is safe contraception on her current effective regimen (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG).

explanation.summary: Any woman of childbearing potential remaining on valproate must be in the TGA Pregnancy Prevention Program: annual specialist counselling, a highly effective contraceptive method (IUD or implant preferred), and documented acknowledgement of teratogenic risk.
key_points: Valproate: ~10% congenital malformation, ~30-40% neurodevelopmental impairment.
Highly effective contraception = LARC (Cu-IUD, LNG-IUD, etonogestrel implant) or DMPA.
Combined oral contraceptive is user-dependent and less preferred here.
explanation.pearls: If she conceives, valproate is a Category D drug and pre-conceptual switch (usually to lamotrigine) is planned with psychiatry.

subtopic_detail: Mood stabiliser choice in first trimester bipolar
stem:
You are the perinatal psychiatry registrar. A 29 year old woman with bipolar I disorder is 7 weeks pregnant. She has been well on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for 3 years after two severe manic episodes.

The pregnancy was unplanned. Her last episode was 3 years ago and required admission and a period of involuntary treatment. She has previously trialled lithium with acceptable tolerance but was switched to valproate for superior symptom control. She has taken folic acid 500 micrograms daily only since finding out she was pregnant last week.

On assessment she is euthymic with intact insight. Blood pressure is 116/72, pulse 74 regular. Booking bloods including TFTs, FBC, LFTs, and renal function are within normal limits. Beta hCG confirms viable intrauterine pregnancy on ultrasound today.

data_table.Investigations: TFTs, FBC, LFTs, renal function within normal limits; viable intrauterine pregnancy at 7 weeks on ultrasound
data_table.Medications: Sodium valproate 1000 mg daily; folic acid 500 micrograms daily (started last week)
data_table.Psychiatric history: Two prior severe manic admissions; well for 3 years on valproate; previous lithium trial tolerated but less effective

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to her medication regimen?

options.text: Stop valproate abruptly and commence olanzapine 10 mg nocte as sole prophylaxis for the remainder of pregnancy
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation of valproate risks acute manic relapse; a cross-titration to an agent she has previously tolerated is safer than sudden switch to olanzapine monotherapy without a proven personal record on that agent (Source: RANZCP Perinatal CPG).

options.text: Continue valproate at the current dose because organogenesis is already underway and switching risks relapse
options.rationale: Continued valproate exposure across the pregnancy compounds the teratogenic and neurodevelopmental burden well beyond the first trimester; switching earlier still reduces cumulative risk (Source: RANZCP Perinatal CPG).

options.text: Cross-titrate valproate to carbamazepine at an equivalent mood stabilising dose to maintain relapse prevention
options.rationale: Carbamazepine is also Category D with neural tube defect risk and enzyme-induction interactions and is not a safer alternative during pregnancy (Source: AMH).

options.text: Cross-titrate valproate to lithium with weekly levels and increase folic acid to 5 mg daily during the switch
options.rationale: Continuing valproate confers ~10% major malformation risk and neurodevelopmental impairment; cross-titration to a mood stabiliser with demonstrable prior tolerability and lower teratogenic burden (lithium ~0.1% Ebstein anomaly) is recommended, with high-dose folate and specialist monitoring (Source: RANZCP Perinatal CPG; AMH).

options.text: Stop valproate and rely on structured psychological therapy alone for mood stabilisation across the pregnancy
options.rationale: Psychological therapy is not adequate mood stabilisation for bipolar I disorder with prior severe mania; the risk of unmedicated relapse is high, particularly in the postpartum (Source: RANZCP Perinatal CPG).

explanation.summary: First trimester valproate carries the highest teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risk of the mood stabilisers. Cross-titrating to a previously tolerated safer agent (usually lithium) minimises cumulative exposure while maintaining relapse prevention; folic acid dose is escalated to 5 mg daily.
key_points: Valproate: 10% major malformation, 30-40% neurodevelopmental effects.
Lithium: ~0.1% Ebstein anomaly, requires close level monitoring especially peripartum.
Abrupt cessation of a mood stabiliser in bipolar I is a high-risk event.
explanation.pearls: The postpartum period is the highest-risk window for bipolar relapse; medication planning must include a postpartum plan.

subtopic_detail: Sodium bicarbonate for QRS widening
stem:
You are the ED registrar. A 24 year old man is brought in 90 minutes after ingesting an unknown quantity of his father's amitriptyline tablets in an argument. He was found drowsy but rousable and had a witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure in the ambulance which self-terminated.

On arrival he is drowsy with GCS 11 (E3 V3 M5), dry mucous membranes, dilated pupils, and warm dry skin. There is no focal neurology and no evidence of trauma. He has no known medical history and is not on any regular medications of his own.

Vital signs: pulse 128 sinus, blood pressure 92/58, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 96% on 4 L nasal prongs, temperature 37.9. Bedside glucose 5.6 mmol/L. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with a QRS duration of 138 ms, dominant R wave in aVR, and a QTc of 480 ms. Venous blood gas: pH 7.29, pCO2 42, HCO3 19, lactate 3.1.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128 sinus, BP 92/58, RR 20, SpO2 96% on 4 L NP, temperature 37.9
data_table.Examination: GCS 11 (E3 V3 M5); dilated pupils; dry warm skin; no focal neurology
data_table.ECG: Sinus tachycardia; QRS 138 ms; dominant R wave in aVR; QTc 480 ms
data_table.Medications: Ingested unknown quantity amitriptyline 90 minutes ago; nil regular

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Give oral activated charcoal 50 g and observe for spontaneous QRS narrowing over the next 4 hours
options.rationale: Charcoal is appropriate within 1-2 hours in an alert cooperative patient but is unsafe here given reduced GCS and seizure risk without airway protection; and it does not address the established cardiotoxicity (Source: eTG Toxicology).

options.text: Give intravenous flumazenil 200 micrograms and repeat as required to reverse the reduced conscious level
options.rationale: Flumazenil is contraindicated in mixed or TCA overdose because it can precipitate seizures and unmask arrhythmias; it has no role here (Source: eTG Toxicology).

options.text: Load intravenous phenytoin 15 mg/kg for seizure prophylaxis given the ingestion and witnessed seizure
options.rationale: Phenytoin shares sodium channel blockade with TCAs and can worsen cardiotoxicity; benzodiazepines are the anticonvulsant of choice in TCA poisoning (Source: eTG Toxicology).

options.text: Commence intravenous amiodarone 300 mg over 20 minutes for the wide complex tachycardia on ECG
options.rationale: Class Ia/Ic and class III antiarrhythmics prolong QT and can precipitate torsades in TCA toxicity; amiodarone is contraindicated (Source: eTG Toxicology).

options.text: Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate 8.4% as a 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus and repeat until the QRS narrows below 100 ms
options.rationale: QRS >100 ms with hypotension and seizure indicates significant sodium channel blockade in TCA toxicity; hypertonic sodium bicarbonate is the first-line antidote and is titrated to QRS narrowing and arterial pH 7.45-7.55 (Source: eTG Toxicology; Australia Poisons Information Centre).

explanation.summary: QRS >100 ms in TCA overdose predicts seizure and ventricular arrhythmia. Hypertonic sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg bolus is titrated to narrowing of the QRS and arterial alkalisation. Class I/III antiarrhythmics and flumazenil are contraindicated.
key_points: QRS >100 ms predicts seizure; >160 ms predicts ventricular arrhythmia.
R wave in aVR >3 mm supports diagnosis.
Benzodiazepines for seizures; hyperventilation and hypertonic saline are adjuncts.
explanation.pearls: Lipid emulsion therapy is a rescue option for refractory cardiovascular collapse in severe TCA toxicity.

subtopic_detail: Varenicline black box warning for a patient with depression history
stem:
You are the GP registrar seeing a 46 year old man who wants to stop smoking. He smokes 25 cigarettes per day and has done so for 25 years. His most recent quit attempt using nicotine patches alone lasted 3 weeks 2 years ago.

He has a history of a single moderate depressive episode 5 years ago that resolved with 12 months of sertraline, ceased 3 years ago; he is currently euthymic with no suicidal ideation and works full time as an electrician. He has no history of seizures, eating disorder, or alcohol use disorder. He has stable angina on aspirin and atorvastatin.

On assessment he is calm and future-focussed. Blood pressure is 132/82, pulse 78 regular. Physical examination is otherwise unremarkable. He asks what the most effective medication for quitting would be.

data_table.Psychiatric history: Single moderate depressive episode 5 years ago; euthymic 3 years; no suicidal ideation
data_table.Medical history: Stable angina; no seizures; no eating disorder; no alcohol use disorder
data_table.Medications: Aspirin 100 mg daily; atorvastatin 40 mg nocte

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Combination nicotine replacement therapy (patch plus lozenge as required) with behavioural support
options.rationale: Combination NRT is effective but varenicline has superior evidence for sustained abstinence in heavy smokers, and the historical EAGLES trial showed no excess neuropsychiatric risk in stable patients (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines).

options.text: Varenicline titrated over the first week to 1 mg twice daily with behavioural support and standard neuropsychiatric monitoring
options.rationale: Varenicline is the most effective single agent and the RACGP guideline reaffirms it as first-line in stable patients regardless of past depression; the black box warning was downgraded after EAGLES demonstrated no excess neuropsychiatric events in stable patients but routine safety monitoring is still advised (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines; AMH).

options.text: Bupropion sustained release 150 mg daily titrated to twice daily with behavioural support and quit date at week 2
options.rationale: Bupropion is a valid second-line option but reduces the seizure threshold and is less effective than varenicline; it is not first-line where varenicline is safe (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines).

options.text: Nortriptyline 25 mg nocte titrated to 75 mg with behavioural support and a set quit date at 2 weeks
options.rationale: Nortriptyline is third-line for smoking cessation, used only when first- and second-line options are contraindicated or have failed (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines).

options.text: Nicotine vaping product prescription with 6 monthly review and no other pharmacotherapy at this stage
options.rationale: Nicotine vaping products are reserved for patients who have failed first-line pharmacotherapy; they are not the initial choice in a treatment-naive patient with an effective option available (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Varenicline is the most effective single-agent smoking cessation pharmacotherapy in Australia. The EAGLES trial found no excess neuropsychiatric events versus NRT or placebo in stable patients with or without prior psychiatric illness; the FDA black box warning was subsequently removed, though monitoring remains prudent.
key_points: First-line: varenicline or combination NRT (patch plus fast acting).
Bupropion is second-line; contraindicated with seizure disorder, eating disorder, or acute alcohol/benzo withdrawal.
Nicotine vaping products are for those who have failed first-line therapy.
explanation.pearls: Prescribe varenicline for 12 weeks minimum; a further 12 weeks reduces relapse in responders.

subtopic_detail: Bupropion contraindication
stem:
You are the GP registrar. A 34 year old woman wants to stop smoking after 15 years of a 20 cigarette a day habit. She has previously used nicotine gum without success.

Her medical history includes anorexia nervosa in her early twenties requiring inpatient treatment, currently in stable recovery, and one witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure last year attributed to sleep deprivation and heavy alcohol use during a stressful period at work. She has since abstained from alcohol and takes no regular medications.

On assessment she is well. Blood pressure is 122/78, pulse 70 regular. BMI 20.1. She is not pregnant and uses a copper IUD. She has read online about bupropion and asks whether it would suit her.

data_table.History: Anorexia nervosa in stable recovery; one unprovoked-appearing seizure last year in context of alcohol and sleep deprivation; alcohol abstinent 12 months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Bupropion sustained release 150 mg daily titrating to 150 mg twice daily with behavioural support
options.rationale: Bupropion is contraindicated in patients with a seizure history and in current or past eating disorder; both are absolute contraindications on the Australian PI (Source: AMH; RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines).

options.text: Nortriptyline 25 mg nocte titrated to 75 mg with behavioural support and a set quit date at week 2
options.rationale: Nortriptyline is third-line, reserved for those who have failed or cannot tolerate first- and second-line therapy (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines).

options.text: Nicotine patch 21 mg daily alone as monotherapy without a fast-acting nicotine product added on
options.rationale: Monotherapy NRT is less effective than combination NRT or varenicline and is not preferred in a patient who has already failed a single nicotine product (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines).

options.text: Varenicline titrated over the first week to 1 mg twice daily with behavioural support and quit date at day 8
options.rationale: Varenicline is a first-line effective option with no seizure or eating-disorder contraindication and is appropriate here where bupropion is contraindicated and gum alone has failed (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines; AMH).

options.text: Behavioural counselling alone without any pharmacotherapy for a further 12 weeks before reconsidering options
options.rationale: Combining behavioural support with pharmacotherapy roughly doubles quit rates compared with either alone; withholding pharmacotherapy in a motivated patient is not appropriate (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Bupropion is contraindicated in seizure history and in current or past eating disorder. Varenicline is first-line where NRT alone has failed and there are no contraindications. Combining pharmacotherapy with behavioural support doubles quit rates.
key_points: Bupropion absolute CIs: seizure disorder, eating disorder, acute alcohol/benzo withdrawal, MAOI.
Varenicline: safe in seizure and eating disorder history; monitor for neuropsychiatric symptoms.
NRT combination (patch + fast-acting) is equivalent to varenicline in many meta-analyses.
explanation.pearls: Pregnancy: NRT is first-line; varenicline and bupropion are not recommended.

subtopic_detail: Prescribing authority and driving in adult ADHD
stem:
You are the GP registrar in NSW. A 28 year old software engineer has been diagnosed with ADHD by a psychiatrist after a formal assessment. Recommendation letter recommends a trial of lisdexamfetamine.

He drives daily to work over the Sydney Harbour Bridge and works from a home office 3 days a week. He has no history of substance use disorder, cardiovascular disease, hypertension, glaucoma, or psychosis. He drinks 4 standard drinks per week.

On assessment he is calm and focused. Blood pressure is 128/78, pulse 72 regular. ECG at the psychiatrist's assessment showed sinus rhythm with a QTc of 400 ms and no structural abnormality on echocardiogram. He asks whether you as his GP can prescribe the stimulant and whether he needs to notify Roads and Maritime Services.

data_table.Cardiac: ECG sinus rhythm; QTc 400 ms; echocardiogram no structural abnormality
data_table.History: No substance use disorder; no cardiovascular disease; no psychosis; no glaucoma
data_table.Occupation: Software engineer; drives daily; works from home 3 days per week

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management approach with respect to prescribing and driving?

options.text: Notify Roads and Maritime Services of the ADHD diagnosis directly under mandatory notification requirements
options.rationale: ADHD itself is not a mandatory notification condition; notification is required only if the patient continues to drive against medical advice with an unsafe condition (Source: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive).

options.text: Write a private prescription for lisdexamfetamine without any regulatory notification given the psychiatrist has assessed him
options.rationale: Any prescriber of a Schedule 8 psychostimulant in NSW must hold or share a stimulant authority; a specialist assessment does not exempt the GP from the regulatory requirement (Source: NSW Health Stimulant Authority).

options.text: Refer him back to the psychiatrist for all ongoing prescribing because GPs are not permitted to prescribe stimulants in NSW
options.rationale: NSW GPs can prescribe under a shared care or delegated authority arrangement once the specialist has initiated and the authority is granted; sole specialist prescribing is not required (Source: NSW Health Stimulant Authority).

options.text: Advise him he must surrender his driver licence for 12 months from the date of starting stimulant medication
options.rationale: Austroads criteria permit private driving on stable therapeutic stimulant dosing without cognitive or behavioural impairment; blanket licence surrender is not required (Source: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive).

options.text: Apply to NSW Health for a Schedule 8 stimulant authority as the primary prescriber before writing any stimulant script
options.rationale: In NSW a stimulant authority under the Poisons and Therapeutic Goods Regulation is required to prescribe Schedule 8 psychostimulants; this can be a co-prescribing arrangement with the specialist, but must be in place before dispensing; driving is generally permitted on stable therapeutic stimulant dosing (Source: NSW Health Stimulant Authority Guidelines; Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive).

explanation.summary: In NSW, Schedule 8 psychostimulants require a stimulant authority under the Poisons and Therapeutic Goods Regulation. GPs can co-prescribe under a shared care model with the initiating specialist. Driving is generally permitted on stable therapeutic stimulant dosing per Austroads.
key_points: NSW stimulant authority is required before dispensing any Schedule 8 stimulant.
Baseline BP, HR, ECG when indicated, and screen for cardiovascular disease before starting.
Austroads permits private driving on stable stimulant dosing without cognitive impairment.
explanation.pearls: Substance use disorder is a relative contraindication to stimulants; consider atomoxetine or guanfacine as non-scheduled alternatives.

subtopic_detail: Second-line stimulant choice in comorbid substance use
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in an outpatient clinic. A 34 year old man with confirmed adult ADHD presents for pharmacotherapy planning. He has never trialled medication.

He has a 6 year history of methamphetamine use disorder in sustained remission for 18 months, engaged with a drug and alcohol counsellor, and has been out of correctional supervision for 2 years. He works as a self-employed carpenter and drives his own ute daily to job sites. He has no psychosis, cardiovascular disease, or hypertension.

On assessment he is calm with intact insight. Blood pressure is 126/78, pulse 72 regular. ECG shows sinus rhythm with QTc 410 ms. Urine drug screen today is negative. He is worried about relapse and asks what medication would be safest for him.

data_table.History: Methamphetamine use disorder in sustained remission 18 months; engaged with counsellor

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Immediate-release dexamfetamine tablets titrated to therapeutic dose with weekly dispense supervision
options.rationale: Immediate-release stimulants have the highest misuse liability and are least preferred in a patient with a history of stimulant use disorder; a long-acting agent or non-stimulant is preferred (Source: RANZCP ADHD Position Statement; eTG Psychotropic).

options.text: Bupropion sustained release 150 mg daily titrated to 300 mg daily as first-line pharmacotherapy for adult ADHD
options.rationale: Bupropion has limited evidence in adult ADHD and is not a first-line agent in Australian guidelines; it is used when other options are contraindicated (Source: RANZCP ADHD Position Statement).

options.text: Atomoxetine titrated over 2 weeks to a maintenance dose of 80 mg daily with 4 to 6 weekly review of efficacy and BP
options.rationale: Atomoxetine is a non-stimulant selective noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor with no misuse potential and is preferred first-line in adults with ADHD and a personal history of stimulant use disorder in stable recovery (Source: RANZCP ADHD Position Statement; eTG Psychotropic).

options.text: Lisdexamfetamine 30 mg daily titrated up as a long-acting stimulant with prodrug formulation reducing misuse risk
options.rationale: Lisdexamfetamine's prodrug status lowers but does not eliminate misuse risk; RANZCP still lists non-stimulants ahead of stimulants when there is a personal history of stimulant use disorder (Source: RANZCP ADHD Position Statement).

options.text: Modafinil 200 mg daily with slow uptitration to 400 mg daily as a wakefulness-promoting agent for ADHD symptoms
options.rationale: Modafinil is not an approved or evidence-based first-line ADHD pharmacotherapy in Australia and is not TGA indicated for ADHD (Source: AMH).

explanation.summary: In adult ADHD with a history of stimulant use disorder in stable remission, non-stimulant pharmacotherapy is preferred first-line. Atomoxetine is TGA-approved for adult ADHD, has no misuse potential, and takes 4-6 weeks for full effect.
key_points: Atomoxetine and guanfacine are non-stimulant options.
Long-acting stimulants (lisdexamfetamine, methylphenidate MR) are preferred over IR when stimulants are used.
Baseline BP, HR, and cardiac history for all stimulant candidates.
explanation.pearls: Atomoxetine carries a rare warning for suicidal ideation in young adults and hepatotoxicity; monitor mood and consider LFTs if symptomatic.

subtopic_detail: Discriminating brief psychotic disorder from schizophreniform and schizophrenia
stem:
You are the community psychiatry registrar. A 26 year old woman is brought in by her partner. She has had 3 weeks of fixed persecutory beliefs that her neighbours are broadcasting her thoughts, disorganised speech, and 2 witnessed episodes of speaking to voices only she can hear.

She has no previous psychiatric history. There was no clear trigger and no bereavement or trauma. She uses no illicit substances (urine drug screen negative) and has not started any new medications. She has been sleeping only 3 to 4 hours a night for the past fortnight.

On examination she is guarded and preoccupied but oriented. Blood pressure is 118/76, pulse 82 regular. Physical examination and routine bloods including TSH, calcium, LFTs, FBC, and CT brain are unremarkable. Her mood is not persistently elevated or depressed and there is no history of prior manic episodes.

data_table.Mental state: Guarded and preoccupied; oriented; persecutory delusions of thought broadcasting; auditory hallucinations; disorganised speech; no persistent mood disturbance
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative; TSH, calcium, LFTs, FBC within normal limits; CT brain normal

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis at this presentation?

options.text: Brief psychotic disorder as psychosis has been present for less than one month total duration
options.rationale: DSM-5-TR brief psychotic disorder requires at least one positive symptom lasting >=1 day but <1 month with eventual full return to premorbid functioning; at 3 weeks she meets duration criteria for brief psychotic disorder pending resolution (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG).

options.text: Schizophreniform disorder as the presentation is typical of an early primary psychotic illness in this age group
options.rationale: Schizophreniform disorder requires 1-6 months of continuous symptoms; at 3 weeks she does not yet meet the minimum duration (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Schizophrenia because thought broadcasting and persistent auditory hallucinations are pathognomonic first rank features
options.rationale: Schizophrenia requires >=6 months of prodrome or active symptoms; first-rank symptoms are neither necessary nor sufficient in DSM-5-TR (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Delusional disorder because the persecutory belief is non bizarre and there are no other prominent symptoms
options.rationale: Delusional disorder requires >=1 month of one or more delusions without prominent hallucinations, disorganised speech, negative symptoms, or grossly disorganised behaviour; the prominent hallucinations and disorganised speech here rule it out (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder given the co-occurrence of sleep disturbance and prominent psychotic features
options.rationale: Schizoaffective disorder requires a major mood episode concurrent with the active phase of psychosis and >=2 weeks of psychosis without prominent mood symptoms; there is no persistent mood disturbance here (Source: DSM-5-TR).

explanation.summary: DSM-5-TR duration thresholds: brief psychotic disorder <1 month, schizophreniform 1-6 months, schizophrenia >=6 months. Delusional disorder requires absence of prominent hallucinations, disorganised speech, or negative symptoms. Schizoaffective requires a concurrent major mood episode.
key_points: Duration is the discriminator between brief psychotic, schizophreniform, and schizophrenia.
Delusional disorder: single non-bizarre or bizarre delusion, no other psychotic features.
Schizoaffective: mood episode concurrent with active psychosis plus >=2 weeks of pure psychosis.
explanation.pearls: Diagnosis is often provisional and may evolve; document trajectory to allow revision at 1 and 6 month marks.

subtopic_detail: Recognising delusional disorder
stem:
You are the GP registrar. A 58 year old woman is brought by her adult daughter because for 15 months she has held the fixed conviction that her husband is having an affair with the next door neighbour. She has hired a private investigator and repeatedly examined his phone.

Outside of this belief her daughter describes her as her usual self: she works part time as a bookkeeper, cooks family meals, maintains her friendships, and has no other unusual beliefs or perceptual experiences. There is no history of depressed or elevated mood, no substance use, and no cognitive decline. She takes atorvastatin and perindopril for cardiovascular risk.

On assessment she is cooperative and detailed. She insists calmly on the reality of her belief and provides ostensibly reasonable explanations for it. Blood pressure is 132/80, pulse 74 regular. MoCA is 28/30. TSH, calcium, LFTs, FBC, B12 and CT brain are within normal limits.

data_table.Mental state: Cooperative; single fixed belief of spousal infidelity; no other delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech, or negative symptoms; euthymic
data_table.Function: Continues part-time work, meal preparation, and social activities
data_table.Investigations: MoCA 28/30; TSH, calcium, LFTs, FBC, B12 within normal limits; CT brain unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Major depressive disorder with psychotic features because the belief indicates mood-congruent delusional thinking
options.rationale: There is no depressed mood, anhedonia, or neurovegetative disturbance; delusion of jealousy is not a mood-congruent feature (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Late onset schizophrenia given the age and the persistence of a fixed non-bizarre belief for more than 6 months
options.rationale: Schizophrenia requires additional active-phase symptoms (hallucinations, disorganised speech, negative symptoms) that are absent here, and functional impairment; these are not present (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Delusional disorder, jealous type, presenting outside of any mood or other psychotic illness
options.rationale: DSM-5-TR delusional disorder requires >=1 month of one or more delusions with function otherwise preserved and no other prominent psychotic symptoms; jealous type describes the delusional infidelity content and duration criteria are exceeded (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Alcohol-induced psychotic disorder given the classical presentation of morbid jealousy in older adults with alcohol use
options.rationale: There is no history of substance use; alcohol-induced psychotic disorder requires temporal relationship to intoxication or withdrawal (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia presenting with disinhibition and fixed erroneous beliefs about her spouse
options.rationale: bvFTD would show progressive personality change, executive dysfunction, apathy, or disinhibition; MoCA of 28/30 and preserved function make bvFTD unlikely (Source: DSM-5-TR).

explanation.summary: Delusional disorder is characterised by one or more delusions of >=1 month duration with function otherwise largely preserved, no prominent hallucinations, disorganised speech, negative symptoms, or grossly disorganised behaviour. Jealous type has spousal infidelity as the delusional content.
key_points: Subtypes: erotomanic, grandiose, jealous, persecutory, somatic, mixed, unspecified.
Function is preserved apart from the impact of the delusion.
Treatment: antipsychotic (often modest doses), engagement often limited.
explanation.pearls: Rule out organic causes (dementia, alcohol, medication-induced) and rule out mood disorder with psychotic features before diagnosing.

subtopic_detail: Synthetic cannabinoid intoxication vs primary psychosis
stem:
You are the ED registrar. A 19 year old university student is brought in by ambulance after collapsing at a music festival. His friend reports he smoked what he called "K2" from a vape 90 minutes before symptoms started.

He has no known psychiatric history. On arrival he is agitated, sweating profusely, and describes visual distortions and paranoid ideation. He has no headache, focal neurology, chest pain, or dysuria. He last ate 4 hours ago and drank 3 beers earlier.

On assessment: pulse 138 regular, blood pressure 168/104, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 39.1. He is agitated but redirectable. Pupils 6 mm equal and reactive. There is a fine tremor and diaphoresis. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with normal intervals. Urine drug screen (immunoassay) is negative for cannabinoids, amphetamines, cocaine and opioids. Creatine kinase is 2400 U/L, sodium 140, potassium 4.0.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138 regular, BP 168/104, RR 24, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 39.1
data_table.Examination: Agitated but redirectable; pupils 6 mm reactive; fine tremor; diaphoresis; no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen (immunoassay) negative for cannabinoids, amphetamines, cocaine, opioids; CK 2400 U/L; sodium 140; potassium 4.0

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Synthetic cannabinoid receptor agonist intoxication with sympathomimetic and agitation features
options.rationale: Synthetic cannabinoids (SCRAs, e.g. "K2", "Spice") are full CB1 agonists producing tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, agitation and psychosis, often with rhabdomyolysis; standard immunoassay does NOT detect them, so a negative cannabinoid screen does not exclude the diagnosis (Source: eTG Toxicology; NCETA Synthetic Cannabinoid Fact Sheet).

options.text: Serotonin syndrome triggered by an undisclosed ingestion of an MDMA-containing tablet at the festival
options.rationale: Serotonin syndrome usually shows hyperreflexia, clonus (especially lower limbs), and ocular clonus; these classical features are not described and MDMA would typically be detected on immunoassay (Source: eTG Toxicology).

options.text: First episode schizophrenia presenting with a substance triggered acute psychotic episode at a festival
options.rationale: The autonomic hyperactivity, hyperthermia, and rhabdomyolysis are inconsistent with primary schizophrenia; toxidrome features and temporal relationship to inhalation of the SCRA drive the diagnosis (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Anticholinergic toxidrome from a novel psychoactive substance sold as a cannabinoid at the festival stall
options.rationale: Anticholinergic toxidrome features dry mucous membranes, urinary retention, absent bowel sounds, and flushed dry skin; this patient is diaphoretic which is against anticholinergic aetiology (Source: eTG Toxicology).

options.text: Acute alcohol withdrawal in a young man now presenting 6 hours after his last drink at the festival
options.rationale: Alcohol withdrawal requires a background of sustained heavy drinking; 3 beers is inadequate substrate and the timeframe of 4 hours from last drink is too short for withdrawal (Source: eTG Toxicology).

explanation.summary: Synthetic cannabinoid receptor agonists (SCRAs, "K2", "Spice") are full CB1 agonists (unlike THC partial agonism), producing severe sympathomimetic toxicity, agitation, psychosis, and rhabdomyolysis. Standard urine cannabinoid immunoassay does not detect them - a negative result does not exclude the diagnosis.
key_points: SCRAs cause more severe toxicity than THC because they are full agonists.
Standard immunoassay does not detect SCRAs; specific testing required.
Management: benzodiazepines for agitation, cooling, IV fluids for rhabdomyolysis.
explanation.pearls: "Bath salts" (synthetic cathinones) are the sympathomimetic parallel to SCRAs; a similar toxidrome with a negative amphetamine screen.

subtopic_detail: Rapid tranquillisation of an acutely disturbed adult
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a metropolitan ED. A 32 year old man with a known diagnosis of schizophrenia is brought in by police after threatening his neighbour with a knife. He is now in a seclusion room and is verbally hostile, pacing, and threatening to punch staff.

He is not on any regular antipsychotic (defaulted 6 months ago) and denies substance use today. Attempts at verbal de-escalation over the past 20 minutes have not settled him. He refuses oral medication.

He weighs approximately 80 kg. There is no known cardiac history, no recent head injury, and no known allergies. Blood pressure taken through the seclusion window is 138/86, pulse 118 regular, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 98% room air. Bedside glucose 5.6 mmol/L. He has not been assessed for QTc as an ECG has not been feasible.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/86, pulse 118 regular, RR 20, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Behaviour: Verbally hostile, pacing, threatening staff; declines oral medication; verbal de-escalation failed after 20 minutes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological approach?

options.text: Intramuscular lorazepam 4 mg as sole first-line therapy for acute behavioural disturbance in this patient
options.rationale: Lorazepam monotherapy is an option but does not treat the underlying psychosis; IM olanzapine is preferred first-line in a known psychotic patient not on regular antipsychotic (Source: RANZCP Acute Behavioural Disturbance Guideline).

options.text: Intramuscular midazolam 10 mg immediately followed by intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg from a separate syringe
options.rationale: Concomitant parenteral olanzapine and benzodiazepine carries a significant risk of respiratory depression and hypotension; TGA and RANZCP warn against this combination (Source: TGA olanzapine PI; RANZCP Acute Behavioural Disturbance Guideline).

options.text: Intramuscular haloperidol 10 mg as a single loading dose without ECG availability given the acuity of the situation
options.rationale: High-dose IM haloperidol without ECG carries a substantial QTc and torsades risk and is not recommended as first-line; IM olanzapine or lower-dose haloperidol with promethazine is preferred where available (Source: RANZCP Acute Behavioural Disturbance Guideline).

options.text: Intramuscular ketamine 4 mg/kg as a rapid dissociative sedative given the failure of verbal de-escalation
options.rationale: Ketamine is reserved for pre-hospital or code-black-style acute severe agitation and requires airway management readiness; it is not first-line for in-hospital psychiatric agitation (Source: RANZCP Acute Behavioural Disturbance Guideline).

options.text: Intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg with a minimum 1 hour interval before considering a repeat dose
options.rationale: RANZCP and NSW Health guidance recommend IM olanzapine 5-10 mg as first-line for acute behavioural disturbance in an adult without benzodiazepine coadministration due to respiratory depression risk; onset ~15-45 min; monitor sedation and vitals (Source: RANZCP Acute Behavioural Disturbance Guideline; NSW Health Management of Adults with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance).

explanation.summary: For acute behavioural disturbance in an adult with known psychosis and after failed de-escalation, IM olanzapine 5-10 mg is first-line per RANZCP and NSW Health. Do NOT combine parenteral olanzapine with parenteral benzodiazepines because of respiratory depression risk.
key_points: IM olanzapine 5-10 mg first-line; onset 15-45 min.
Do not co-administer parenteral olanzapine with parenteral benzodiazepine.
IM droperidol or IM haloperidol + promethazine are alternatives where olanzapine is unavailable.
explanation.pearls: Post-sedation observations: pulse, BP, respiratory rate, SpO2, and level of consciousness every 15 minutes until fully alert.

subtopic_detail: DBT skill selection for acute distress
stem:
You are the community psychiatry registrar. A 27 year old woman with a diagnosis of borderline personality disorder attends her scheduled DBT session in acute distress after an argument with her partner.

She describes an urge to cut her forearm which she rates 9/10, tearfulness, and an impulse to "do something to feel real". She denies suicidal ideation or a plan. She is not currently intoxicated, has no acute medical concerns, and has attended 4 months of the DBT program.

On assessment she is tearful but engageable and cooperative with the session. She has completed the mindfulness module and is currently working through distress tolerance. She asks which skill she should use right now to get through the next hour without self-harming.

data_table.Presentation: Acute distress after interpersonal conflict; urge to self-harm 9/10; denies suicidal ideation
data_table.Treatment: 4 months into DBT; completed mindfulness module; currently in distress tolerance module

lead_in: Which DBT skill is most appropriate for her to use in the next hour?

options.text: DEAR MAN interpersonal effectiveness skill to negotiate a resolution with her partner about the argument now
options.rationale: DEAR MAN is an interpersonal effectiveness skill best used when arousal is manageable; at 9/10 urge intensity, distress tolerance must precede interpersonal engagement (Source: Linehan DBT Skills Manual 2nd Ed).

options.text: TIPP skills (temperature, intense exercise, paced breathing, paired muscle relaxation) to rapidly reduce arousal
options.rationale: TIPP is Linehan's crisis survival skill within distress tolerance, designed for very high emotional arousal (>=7/10) to rapidly reduce sympathetic activation via the dive reflex, aerobic exertion, and paced breathing; onset within minutes and appropriate to bridge the next hour (Source: Linehan DBT Skills Training Manual 2nd Ed; RANZCP Personality Disorders CPG).

options.text: Radical acceptance to acknowledge the reality of the conflict as the primary short-term response now
options.rationale: Radical acceptance is a reality acceptance skill for longer-term suffering, not the acute crisis survival skill needed when the urge to self-harm is 9/10 (Source: Linehan DBT Skills Manual 2nd Ed).

options.text: Check the facts from the emotion regulation module to appraise the argument objectively before acting
options.rationale: Check the facts is an emotion regulation skill useful once arousal has been reduced; at very high arousal, distress tolerance skills come first (Source: Linehan DBT Skills Manual 2nd Ed).

options.text: Wise mind observation from the core mindfulness module as the primary intervention to prevent the self harm
options.rationale: Mindfulness skills are foundational but not sufficient at 9/10 acute urge; crisis survival distress tolerance is the immediate need (Source: Linehan DBT Skills Manual 2nd Ed).

explanation.summary: DBT crisis survival skills are the immediate intervention when emotional arousal is very high (>=7/10). TIPP (Temperature via cold water dive reflex, Intense exercise, Paced breathing, Paired muscle relaxation) rapidly reduces sympathetic drive within minutes.
key_points: DBT four modules: mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness.
Crisis survival skills (TIPP, ACCEPTS, self-soothe, IMPROVE the moment, pros and cons) sit within distress tolerance.
Interpersonal and emotion regulation skills come AFTER arousal is reduced.
explanation.pearls: TIPP temperature = cold water immersion of the face (dive reflex); avoid in cardiac disease or eating disorder with bradycardia.

subtopic_detail: Pharmacotherapy limits in BPD per NHMRC
stem:
You are the community psychiatry registrar. A 24 year old woman with borderline personality disorder is currently on quetiapine 300 mg nocte, sertraline 100 mg daily, and lorazepam 1 mg PRN twice weekly, all started over the last 12 months by different clinicians during acute crises. She has never had a manic episode or a primary psychotic disorder.

She has gained 8 kg over 6 months and reports daytime sedation. She has not engaged with structured psychological therapy and asks whether she really needs so many medications. There is no current suicidal ideation, no episode of self-harm in the last 6 weeks, and no comorbid substance use disorder.

On assessment she is euthymic. Blood pressure is 128/78, pulse 72 regular. Fasting glucose is 5.6 mmol/L, HbA1c 5.7%, LDL 3.4 mmol/L, triglycerides 1.6 mmol/L. She is otherwise well.

data_table.Fasting bloods: Glucose 5.6 mmol/L; HbA1c 5.7%; LDL 3.4 mmol/L; triglycerides 1.6 mmol/L
data_table.Medications: Quetiapine 300 mg nocte; sertraline 100 mg daily; lorazepam 1 mg PRN twice weekly
data_table.Psychiatric history: BPD; no manic or primary psychotic episodes; no substance use disorder; no recent self-harm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her pharmacological management?

options.text: Continue current medications unchanged given clinical stability and reassess in 12 months for streamlining
options.rationale: Continuing unnecessary polypharmacy is not neutral; metabolic side effects and dependence risk accumulate without symptom benefit (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline).

options.text: Increase quetiapine to 600 mg nocte to address the affective instability more effectively while she waits for therapy
options.rationale: Escalating quetiapine adds metabolic and sedation burden without robust evidence for BPD core symptoms; deprescribing and prioritising psychotherapy is the guideline direction (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline).

options.text: Structured deprescribing plan targeting all three agents while enrolling her in a formal psychological therapy program
options.rationale: The NHMRC BPD Guideline states that no medication has robust evidence for treating core BPD symptoms; polypharmacy in BPD is common and harmful and should be systematically deprescribed while ensuring access to structured psychological therapy (DBT, MBT, schema therapy) (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline; RANZCP Personality Disorders CPG).

options.text: Substitute lamotrigine for quetiapine because mood stabilisers have proven efficacy for BPD emotional dysregulation
options.rationale: Cochrane and NHMRC reviews (including the LABILE trial) found lamotrigine no more effective than placebo for BPD symptoms; substitution is not supported (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline; LABILE trial).

options.text: Convert PRN lorazepam to scheduled diazepam 5 mg twice daily to reduce impulsive PRN use and taper later
options.rationale: Scheduling benzodiazepines creates dependence and worsens impulsivity and self-harm risk in BPD; both drug class and pattern are contraindicated (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline).

explanation.summary: The NHMRC BPD Guideline recommends structured psychological therapy as the primary treatment for BPD. No medication has robust evidence for core BPD symptoms; polypharmacy is common and harmful and should be systematically deprescribed. Benzodiazepines are contraindicated.
key_points: Structured psychological therapy (DBT, MBT, schema, TFP) is first-line.
Medication has a role only for comorbid conditions (MDD, PTSD) or short-term crisis.
Avoid benzodiazepines; deprescribe polypharmacy systematically.
explanation.pearls: Comorbid conditions (MDD, PTSD, ADHD) are treated on their own merits; do not medicate BPD itself as if it were a mood disorder.

subtopic_detail: Clozapine myocarditis surveillance in the first month
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a clozapine clinic. A 31 year old man is 3 weeks into clozapine titration for treatment-resistant schizophrenia, currently on 200 mg nocte. He has been well through titration and his neutrophils and other bloods have been within target range weekly.

Over the past 3 days he has felt increasingly fatigued, with a low grade fever peaking at 37.9, and mild ankle swelling. He denies chest pain, orthopnoea, syncope, or productive cough. He has no rash, no dysuria, and no diarrhoea.

On examination he is well perfused. Pulse 108 regular, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 37.9. Heart sounds are dual with no murmur; JVP is not raised. Chest is clear. Ankles show mild bilateral pitting. Baseline (pre-clozapine) troponin, CRP, ECG, and echocardiogram were within normal limits. Today: high sensitivity troponin 82 ng/L (<14), CRP 68 mg/L (<5), ECG sinus tachycardia at 108 with 1 mm ST depression in lateral leads. FBC and neutrophils are within the target range.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108 regular, BP 118/72, RR 18, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 37.9
data_table.Examination: Well perfused; dual heart sounds no murmur; JVP not raised; chest clear; mild bilateral ankle pitting
data_table.Investigations today: Troponin 82 ng/L (<14); CRP 68 mg/L (<5); ECG sinus tachycardia 108 with 1 mm lateral ST depression; FBC and neutrophils within target range
data_table.Baseline (pre-clozapine): Troponin, CRP, ECG, echocardiogram within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Clozapine 200 mg nocte, week 3 of titration

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Cease clozapine immediately and refer urgently to cardiology for echocardiogram and troponin trend
options.rationale: Active clozapine myocarditis surveillance criteria (typically Ronaldson protocol adopted by Australian services) are met: tachycardia and troponin above local upper limit with CRP >50 during the first month; the response is immediate cessation, cardiology consultation, and echocardiogram (Source: NSW Health Clozapine Guideline; Ronaldson clozapine myocarditis protocol).

options.text: Continue clozapine at 200 mg nocte and repeat troponin and CRP in 48 hours with symptomatic review
options.rationale: In active surveillance during the high-risk 4 week window, tachycardia plus rising troponin and CRP meets Australian clozapine myocarditis criteria and requires immediate cessation and cardiology assessment (Source: NSW Health Clozapine Guideline for the Management of Physical Health; Ronaldson et al. protocol).

options.text: Halve clozapine to 100 mg nocte, add oral prednisolone 25 mg daily and repeat bloods in 24 hours
options.rationale: Dose reduction does not reverse an inflammatory myocarditis and steroids are not routinely indicated as an outpatient response; cessation and cardiology-led management are required (Source: NSW Health Clozapine Guideline).

options.text: Continue clozapine and start ivabradine to control the sinus tachycardia symptomatically over the next week
options.rationale: Rate-controlling a compensatory tachycardia risks masking clinical deterioration; the priority is to establish or exclude myocarditis, not to blunt vital signs (Source: NSW Health Clozapine Guideline).

options.text: Add oral amoxicillin/clavulanate and continue clozapine as the picture likely represents an intercurrent chest infection
options.rationale: The clinical picture with troponin and CRP rises in the first month on clozapine is myocarditis until proven otherwise; presumptive antibiotics for a clear chest do not address the diagnosis (Source: NSW Health Clozapine Guideline).

explanation.summary: Clozapine-induced myocarditis peaks in the first 4 weeks of titration. Active surveillance is standard in Australian services with weekly troponin, CRP, and clinical review. Any two of: persistent tachycardia >100, troponin above upper limit, CRP >50, or new symptoms (fatigue, fever, dyspnoea) mandates cessation and cardiology consultation.
key_points: Highest myocarditis risk is weeks 2-3 of titration.
Australian surveillance: weekly troponin and CRP plus symptom review for first 4 weeks.
Cessation is required at threshold; rechallenge is specialist-led with cardiology approval.
explanation.pearls: Neutropenia surveillance is a separate weekly requirement; both toxicities have distinct thresholds and neither can be substituted for the other.

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing akathisia from anxiety in first-episode psychosis
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a first-episode psychosis service. A 22 year old man was started on risperidone 2 mg nocte 10 days ago for a first psychotic episode after 3 months of persecutory beliefs and auditory hallucinations. His positive symptoms are beginning to settle.

Over the past 3 days he reports an inner sense of restlessness that is worse in the evening, cannot sit through a 30 minute TV programme, and has to keep pacing his room. He denies persecutory ideas driving the pacing and says he feels physically compelled to move rather than mentally driven. Sleep and appetite are unchanged and there is no current substance use.

On assessment he shifts weight from foot to foot when standing and taps his feet when seated. His mental state is otherwise settling from admission. Pulse 84 regular, blood pressure 122/76, respiratory rate 16, temperature 36.7. Bedside glucose 5.2 mmol/L; TSH within normal limits. He asks if his medication could be the cause.

data_table.Examination: Weight-shifting when standing; foot-tapping when seated; no tremor; no lead-pipe rigidity; no ocular movement abnormality
data_table.Onset: Restlessness onset day 7-8 of risperidone; worse in the evening
data_table.Symptom character: Inner sense of being compelled to move; not driven by persecutory content
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 5.2 mmol/L; TSH within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Add propranolol 20 mg twice daily and reduce risperidone to 1 mg nocte with review at 1 week
options.rationale: Akathisia is best managed by dose reduction of the causative agent plus beta-blockade (propranolol 20-40 mg BD-TDS is the first-line treatment per eTG Psychotropic and Barnes Akathisia Scale-guided practice); onset within days is characteristic (Source: eTG Psychotropic; Barnes Akathisia Rating Scale references).

options.text: Increase risperidone to 3 mg nocte to more rapidly control residual anxiety-driven psychomotor agitation
options.rationale: The picture is akathisia; increasing the causative D2 antagonist will worsen it, not improve it (Source: eTG Psychotropic; RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG).

options.text: Add benztropine 2 mg orally twice daily as first-line pharmacological management of the movement symptoms
options.rationale: Anticholinergics such as benztropine are first-line for acute dystonia and drug-induced parkinsonism, not akathisia; they are unreliable for akathisia and add anticholinergic burden (Source: eTG Psychotropic).

options.text: Commence diazepam 5 mg twice daily as the primary anxiolytic for what most likely represents psychosis-related anxiety
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines can be adjunctive if beta-blockade is contraindicated, but they are not first-line; anchoring on "anxiety" misses the drug-induced mechanism and delays reduction of the D2 antagonist (Source: eTG Psychotropic).

options.text: Cross-titrate risperidone to haloperidol because a higher potency typical antipsychotic will settle the restlessness
options.rationale: Haloperidol has a higher rate of extrapyramidal side effects including akathisia; switching to a higher-potency typical worsens the mechanism, not improves it (Source: AMH).

explanation.summary: Akathisia is a drug-induced sense of inner restlessness with observable psychomotor manifestations (foot-tapping, weight-shifting), typically emerging days to weeks after starting or dose-escalating a D2 antagonist. First-line management is reduction of the causative agent plus propranolol.
key_points: Akathisia: inner restlessness + observable movement; distinguish from anxiety by the physical compulsion to move.
Onset days to weeks after starting/increasing D2 antagonist; worse with higher potency agents.
First-line: dose reduction + propranolol 20-40 mg BD-TDS; second-line: benzodiazepines, mirtazapine, cyproheptadine.
explanation.pearls: Akathisia is associated with medication non-adherence and elevated suicide risk in first-episode psychosis; recognise and treat early.
